👉Tonight might be one of those rare skywatching moments you’ll remember for years.

Comet C/2026 A1 (MAPS) is making its closest approach to the Sun today. If the comet becomes bright enough, there’s a chance you could spot it with the naked eye. Look for a soft glowing patch of light with a faint tail appearing just above the western horizon.

How to watch the comet

→ Step outside about 30 minutes after sunset
→ Face west and scan the sky close to the horizon
→ Allow your eyes 2–3 minutes to adjust to the darkness
→ Watch for a dim, fuzzy glow that doesn’t blink

This isn’t a star, and it isn’t a planet.
It’s a comet racing past the Sun at nearly 150,000 miles per hour.

Did you manage to see it tonight? 👇

By studying these transits, scientists were able to analyze how the planet reflects light. Researchers used Hubble’s imaging spectrograph to track subtle changes in the planet’s light before, during, and after it moved behind its star. According to researcher Frederic Pont, the light became dimmer specifically in the blue wavelengths, while remaining mostly unchanged in green and red. This is a great opportunity to enjoy a rare and beautiful planetary lineup—perfect for both beginners and experienced skywatchers. #space #science #fblifestyle #facts #stargazingExploratory World3.5K views · 8h ago0:11👉During the partial solar eclipse on March 29, 2025, the Sun took on a striking and unusual shape, appearing like glowing “devil horns” in the sky. This dramatic effect happened at sunrise, when the Moon moved across the Sun’s surface and transformed its light into a sharp, uneven crescent that looked both beautiful and slightly eerie. The eclipse was visible across many parts of the Northern Hemisphere, including North America, Europe, and areas around the North Atlantic. People watching from eastern regions during sunrise witnessed the most intense visual effect, while those in higher latitudes experienced up to 80–90% of the Sun being covered at the peak of the event, which lasted several hours. As the Moon partially blocked the Sun, it didn’t fully cover it. Instead, it left behind a thin, glowing arc just above the horizon. Because of the way Earth’s atmosphere bends light during sunrise, this arc appeared distorted, creating two bright points that looked like fiery horns rising from the horizon. Scientifically, this “horns” effect is a combination of orbital alignment and atmospheric refraction. When the Sun is low in the sky, light passes through more of Earth’s atmosphere, which enhances contrast and slightly warps what we see. This can turn a simple crescent into a much more dramatic and exaggerated shape. Although the eclipse lasted only a short time, it left a powerful impression. It was a reminder that even something as familiar as a sunrise can suddenly look strange and otherworldly, showing how our view of the universe can shift in surprising ways. #sun #moon #fblifestyle #eclipse #cosmosExploratory World1.4K views · 8h ago2:00☄️ A Bright Visitor in the Night Sky — Comet C/2025 R3 A recently discovered comet, C/2025 R3, is set to shine at its brightest around April 26, 2026. As it travels through the inner solar system, there’s a good chance it could become visible to the naked eye. This comet was first spotted by advanced sky surveys that track faint moving objects among distant stars. Scientists have calculated that it follows a long, stretched-out orbit—common for comets that originate far beyond the planets. As it gets closer to the Sun (a point called perihelion), heat causes its icy core to release gas and dust. This creates a glowing cloud, known as a coma, along with a long, luminous tail that can extend millions of kilometers into space. As the comet moves nearer to both the Sun and Earth, its brightness is expected to increase, making it easier to spot—especially in clear, dark skies. What makes this event truly exciting is how easy it may be to observe. Unlike many space objects that require telescopes, this comet could be seen with the naked eye. Over several nights, you may even notice it slowly shifting its position in the sky, offering a rare chance to watch a celestial object evolve in real time. However, comets can be unpredictable. Their brightness can suddenly change due to bursts of activity on their surface, where jets of gas and dust erupt into space. This means the comet could appear brighter—or dimmer—than expected, making each observation unique and valuable for scientists. As April approaches, Comet C/2025 R3 will become a faint yet fascinating traveler from the distant edges of our solar system. It carries ancient material preserved for billions of years, giving us a glimpse into the early history of our cosmic neighborhood. ✨ For a short time, this icy wanderer will remind us that the universe is always moving—and sometimes, it puts on a show just for us. #Space #Astronomy #Comet #NightSky #Cosmos #ScienceExploratory World243 views · 11h ago4:25🪐 Rare Sky Week — Mid-April 2026 This week isn’t about just one sky event—it’s a series of beautiful alignments happening over a few mornings and evenings. As Earth continues its journey around the Sun, our viewpoint lines up several planets along the ecliptic (the path the Sun appears to follow). This creates a rare opportunity to spot multiple planets within a short span of time. --- 🌙 April 15 — Moon, Jupiter & Uranus A slim crescent Moon will appear close to Jupiter, with Uranus faintly visible nearby. This moment highlights how quickly the Moon moves in its orbit, passing different planets in just a few nights. --- 🌅 April 18 — Multi-Planet Alignment Just before sunrise, look toward the horizon to see Mercury, Venus, Saturn, and Neptune forming a gentle alignment. This view reflects the flat, disk-like shape of our solar system. --- ✨ What’s Really Happening? These planets aren’t actually close to each other in space. They only appear aligned from our point of view on Earth—a result of orbital motion and perspective. --- 🔭 Why It’s Worth Watching • Helps you visualize the solar system’s ecliptic plane • Shows why planets seem to “line up” in the sky • Lets you compare brightness and distance of different planets • Demonstrates how fast the Moon moves compared to others • Encourages watching the sky over multiple days for the full experience --- 💫 A Bigger Cosmic View No single night captures the entire story. Moments like this are special—they bring distant worlds together in a way that reminds us how vast yet connected our universe is. 🌙✨🔭 #Moon #Venus #Jupiter #Mars #PlanetAlignment #fblifestyle #SkyWatchExploratory World6.9K views · 15h ago0:11😯👉🚨 The James Webb Space Telescope has revealed one of the most exciting clues yet in the search for life beyond Earth! Scientists studying the distant exoplanet K2-18 b, located about 120 light-years away in the constellation Leo, have identified key gases in its atmosphere—methane and carbon dioxide—along with a possible sign of dimethyl sulfide (DMS). On Earth, this molecule is mainly produced by living organisms, especially tiny marine life like plankton. K2-18 b lies within the habitable zone of its star, meaning conditions there could allow liquid water to exist. Researchers believe it might be a “Hycean world”—a planet covered by a vast ocean beneath a thick, hydrogen-rich atmosphere, where simple life forms could potentially survive. This discovery was made by studying how starlight changes as it passes through the planet’s atmosphere during a transit. These subtle changes help scientists identify the chemical makeup of the planet. Although this is not confirmed proof of life yet, the combination of these gases makes K2-18 b one of the most promising places ever found in the search for extraterrestrial life. Scientists will continue observing the planet with the James Webb Space Telescope to verify the presence of DMS and understand its origin.
